title: Position: Neglecting the Sustainability of AI is Fuelling a Global AI Arms Race
claim: Compute capacity and investment are extremely concentrated in a few countries, leaving most of the world far behind.
layout: 2 stacked panels: choropleth world map above, ranked horizontal bar chart below
description: Two stacked data panels. The top panel is a world choropleth map of supercomputer compute capacity per country (PFLOP/s), using a diverging red-to-blue colour scale from 0 to 7,000. The United States is dark navy and stands out immediately. Germany, Japan and Italy are lighter blue. Most other countries are red, and countries with no data (most of Africa, Central Asia and Latin America) are grey and hatched. A horizontal colourbar labelled PFLOP/s sits under the map. The bottom panel is a ranked horizontal bar chart of the top 20 countries by 2024 AI investment, in billion USD. The US bar is about 109.1, and the next country, China, is about 9.29. The long tail shrinks to under 1. The bars reuse the map's colours, so the two panels link visually. Value labels sit at the end of each bar. The eye goes first to the dark US on the map, then to the very long US bar.
caption: Compute capacity (top) in different countries based on the Top500 listing of supercomputers per November, 2025 [ref]. Top 20 countries (bottom) AI investment for 2024 using data derived from [ref].
abstract: Sustainability encompasses three key facets: economic, environmental, and social. However, the nascent discourse on sustainable artificial intelligence (AI) predominantly focuses on the environmental sustainability of AI, neglecting the economic and social aspects. Achieving truly sustainable AI necessitates addressing the tension between its environmental sustainability, which emphasises mitigating AI's climate impact, and its social sustainability, hinging on equitable access to AI development resources. This push for increased accessibility, however, often overlooks the environmental costs of expanding such resource usage. This position paper argues that reconciling climate awareness and resource awareness is essential to realising truly sustainable AI, and neglecting these factors fuels a global AI arms race. Applying Karl Marx's base-superstructure framework from historical materialism, we analyse how the material conditions are shaping the current AI progress and the discourse surrounding it. Further, we introduce the Climate and Resource Aware Machine Learning (CARAML) framework with actionable recommendations spanning individual, community, industry, government, and global levels to achieve sustainable AI.
